encodingDesc.p: The source covers selected passages. Greek text is used solely for exact line matching; canonical Greek is unchanged. Source line identifiers and card milestones are retained, including anomalous numbering. These machine-generated annotations have not received a scholarly correctness review.

seg.head: Line 10

p.quote: ἐν πέντε σισύραις ἐγκεκορδυλημένος.

seg.p: The phrase ἐγκεκορδυλημένος is a hapax legomenon in the extant corpus of Aristophanes, derived from κώρδυλος (a type of coarse, rough woolen garment or, more broadly, a shaggy cloak). The perfect middle/passive participle suggests a state of being 'shrouded' or 'wrapped up' in these five 'sisyrai' (a specific, likely rustic, type of woolen cloak or mantle). The construction is syntactically straightforward but semantically opaque without knowledge of the specific material culture of the term σίσυρα, which appears elsewhere only in comic fragments or glosses, indicating a deliberate use of archaic or technical vocabulary to characterize the subject's ragged, impoverished, or rustic appearance, fitting the play's satire of the Sophists' ascetic affectations.

seg.head: Line 31

p.quote: τρεῖς μναῖ διφρίσκου καὶ τροχοῖν Ἀμυνίᾳ.

seg.p: The phrase 'διφρίσκου' is a hapax legomenon in Aristophanes, appearing only here in the extant corpus. While the verb is derived from the noun διφρίσκος (a type of light, two-wheeled cart), the verbal form is exceptionally rare and its precise semantic nuance here—whether implying a specific type of motion or simply 'to drive'—is debated. The accusative singular 'διφρίσκου' is grammatically regular as the direct object of the implied verb of giving or spending (understood from context), but the rarity of the lexical item itself warrants note for a specialist audience.

seg.head: Line 33

p.quote: ἀλλʼ ὦ μέλʼ ἐξήλικας ἐμέ γʼ ἐκ τῶν ἐμῶν,

seg.p: The vocative form μέλ' (for μέλι) is a rare instance of the elision of the final iota in the vocative of this noun, which is otherwise typically uncontracted or treated differently in comedy; this metrical concession highlights the speaker's emotional outburst and the intimate, abusive address typical of Aristophanic dialogue.

seg.head: Line 46

p.quote: ἔπειτʼ ἔγημα Μεγακλέους τοῦ Μεγακλέους

seg.p: The double use of the name Μεγακλέους (genitive of Megacles) is a deliberate comic device highlighting the absurdity of the name's recurrence within a single phrase, a technique characteristic of Aristophanic wordplay where the repetition serves to mock the speaker's pretension or the obscurity of the genealogy. This specific construction echoes a known comedic trope found elsewhere in the play (e.g., 545) where the repetition of a name is used to satirize the pedantic enumeration of lineage.

seg.head: Line 48

p.quote: σεμνὴν τρυφῶσαν ἐγκεκοισυρωμένην.

seg.p: The participle ἐγκεκοισυρωμένην (from ἐγκεκοισυρῶ) is a hapax legomenon in extant Greek literature, denoting a specific type of disheveled, wind-blown, or 'wind-blowing' state, here metaphorically describing the clouds' unruly, stormy appearance. Its rarity and unique compound formation warrant attention as a deliberate Aristophanic coinage to evoke the chaotic physicality of the Clouds.

seg.head: Line 65

p.quote: ἐγὼ δὲ τοῦ πάππου ʼτιθέμην Φειδωνίδην.

seg.p: The genitive τοῦ πάππου is not merely possessive but denotes the specific familial line or house (the Φειδωνίδαι) from which the speaker claims descent. In Old Comedy, this construction often signals a claim to aristocratic lineage or a specific political faction, here likely alluding to the Pheidonid clan, a prominent family in Athenian history known for figures like Pheidon of Argos (though the Athenian connection is the point of the joke or claim). The use of the proper name in the genitive as a substantive (Φειδωνίδην) functioning as the predicate of ʼτιθέμην (I was counted/set as) is a concise way of asserting identity within that lineage, a rhetorical device common in self-definition within the parabasis or character introductions.

seg.head: Line 96

p.quote: λέγοντες ἀναπείθουσιν ὡς ἔστιν πνιγεύς,

seg.p: The term πνιγεύς (pniugeus) is a hapax legomenon in Aristophanes, appearing only here in the extant corpus. Derived from πνίγειν (to choke), it is a coinage satirizing the Sophists' tendency to invent technical-sounding terminology for trivial or absurd concepts. The word functions as a pun on the physical act of choking (perhaps alluding to the 'strangling' of logic in eristic debates) and the intellectual 'suffocation' of the student, a typical Aristophanic device of lexical invention to mock the perceived obscurantism of contemporary intellectuals.

seg.head: Line 156

p.quote: ἀνήρετʼ αὐτὸν Χαιρεφῶν ὁ Σφήττιος

seg.p: The aorist indicative ἀνήρετ' (from ἀναίρω, 'to lift up' or 'to slay') is metrically contracted here to fit the iambic trimeter; the form ἀνήρεν would be expected in the uncontracted sequence, but the elision of the final nu before the vowel of the following name Χαιρεφῶν is standard in the comic tradition. The verb's usage here, implying 'to kill' or 'to murder' rather than the more common 'to lift up,' is a specific semantic development in Aristophanic comedy, often associated with the chaotic violence of the trial scenes in the Clouds.

seg.head: Line 158

p.quote: κατὰ τὸ στόμʼ ᾄδειν ἢ κατὰ τοὐρροπύγιον.

seg.p: The phrase κατὰ τοὐρροπύγιον ('in the rump-hole') presents a striking example of Aristophanic bathos, juxtaposing the elevated act of singing (ᾄδειν) with the most vulgar anatomical location. The construction κατὰ + accusative here denotes the manner or locus of the action with aggressive physicality, a hallmark of the comic genre's subversion of the 'mouth' (στόμʼ) as the proper organ for vocal performance. This specific collocation appears in the Clouds (line 1338) during the contest between the Just and Unjust Logos, where the Unjust Logos argues that one should sing from the anus to avoid the 'moral' constraints of the mouth, a grotesque inversion of the philosophical ideal of the 'speaking head' versus the 'thinking body'.

seg.head: Line 160

p.quote: ἔφασκεν εἶναι τοὔντερον τῆς ἐμπίδος

seg.p: The phrase τοὔντερον is a crasis of τὸ ἔντερον, literally 'the inside part' or 'the innards.' In this context, where Strepsiades is mocking Socrates' astronomical theories, the term is used ironically to refer to the Earth (or perhaps the celestial sphere) as a physical object located 'inside' or 'at the bottom' of the cosmos, contrasting with the traditional view of the Earth as the central, stable ground. The specific choice of ἔντερον (often associated with entrails) rather than a more standard geographical term like μέση or γῆ adds a layer of grotesque physicality to the comic description of the cosmos, suggesting the Earth is merely a bloated organ within the larger body of the universe, a metaphor consistent with the play's satirical treatment of natural philosophy.

seg.head: Line 168

p.quote: ὅστις δίοιδε τοὔντερον τῆς ἐμπίδος.

seg.p: The form δίοιδε is a Doric aorist indicative active of διόιδω (to go through), contrasting with the Attic δίοισεν. In Aristophanes' comic dialect, this Doricism is a deliberate marker of the rustic character Strepsiades, who is being mocked for his lack of sophistication, while the verb itself is rare in Attic prose, appearing primarily in dialectal or comic contexts to denote a vigorous, often clumsy, passage through a space.

seg.head: Line 171

p.quote: ζητοῦντος αὐτοῦ τῆς σελήνης τὰς ὁδοὺς

seg.p: The construction employs the genitive absolute (ζητοῦντος αὐτοῦ τῆς σελήνης τὰς ὁδοὺς) with a transitive verb (ζητεῖν) governing a direct object (τὰς ὁδοὺς) while the subject of the participle is the same as the implied subject of the main clause. This is syntactically irregular because the genitive absolute typically requires the subject of the participle to be distinct from the subject of the main clause; here, it functions almost as a nominative absolute or a causal clause with a shared subject, a feature rare in Aristophanes and potentially reflecting a specific stylistic license or a corruption in the transmitted text.

seg.head: Line 174

p.quote: ἥσθην γαλεώτῃ καταχέσαντι Σωκράτους.

seg.p: The phrase καταχέσαντι is an aorist active participle of καταχέω, 'to pour down' or 'to drench,' used here in a comic, hyperbolic sense to describe the act of dousing Socrates with water as part of the punishment for his 'theological' inquiries. The construction employs a dative of agent with the aorist participle, a rare syntactic choice in Attic prose but characteristic of Aristophanic comic exaggeration, where the participle functions almost as a verbal noun of action. The use of γαλεώτῃ, 'with a water-skin,' further underscores the absurdity of the scene, as it implies a crude, almost animalistic method of punishment.

The verb ἥσθην, the aorist passive of ἄρχω, is here used in a non-standard sense, meaning 'to be drenched' or 'to be soaked,' rather than its usual meaning of 'to begin' or 'to rule.' This usage is a rare and deliberate comic distortion of the verb, typical of Aristophanes' linguistic playfulness, and serves to emphasize the physical and metaphorical 'drowning' of Socrates in the context of the Clouds' judgment.

seg.head: Line 186

p.quote: τοῖς ἐκ Πύλου ληφθεῖσι τοῖς Λακωνικοῖς.

seg.p: The phrase refers to the Spartan hoplites captured by the Athenians after the disaster at Sphacteria in 425 BCE, an event that precipitated a constitutional crisis in Sparta due to the large number of Spartiates held hostage. The perfect passive participle ληφθεῖσι (from λαμβάνω) emphasizes the resulting state of being held captive rather than the moment of capture, which is crucial for understanding the political leverage Athens momentarily held over Sparta and the specific context of the Athenian threat being invoked in the play.

seg.head: Line 192

p.quote: οὗτοι δʼ ἐρεβοδιφῶσιν ὑπὸ τὸν Τάρταρον.

seg.p: The compound verb ἐρεβοδιφῶσιν is a rare hapax legomenon (or near-hapax in the surviving corpus) formed from ἔρεβος ('darkness') and δίφω ('I scratch'). The term functions as a vivid, onomatopoeic coinage by Aristophanes to describe the frantic scratching or digging sound of the cloud-chariot's wheels or the charioteers' frantic movements in the underworld, rather than a standard term for 'digging'. Its morphology and semantic construction exemplify the comic poet's tendency to create new compounds to match the specific auditory or visual grotesquerie of the scene.

seg.head: Line 218

p.quote: φέρε τίς γὰρ οὗτος οὑπὶ τῆς κρεμάθρας ἀνήρ;

seg.p: The phrase 'οὑπὶ τῆς κρεμάθρας' presents a crux of textual criticism and syntactic interpretation. While 'κρεμάθρα' (a hanging basket or sieve) is attested, the prepositional phrase 'οὑπὶ' (a crasis of 'ὁ ἐπί') followed by the genitive is highly irregular for Aristophanes' typical usage, where 'ἐπί' usually governs the accusative for motion toward or the dative for location. Some editors, following a conjecture by Hermann, have suggested emending 'οὑπὶ' to 'ἐν' or reinterpreting the case as a rare dative construction implying 'under the influence of' the basket, reflecting a metaphorical 'hanging' state of confusion or intoxication. This syntactic irregularity is compounded by the ambiguity of 'κρεμάθρα' itself: while literally a hanging basket, in this comedic context it may allude to a specific prop or a metaphorical device for the 'Clouds' themselves, whose suspended nature is central to the play's satire of Socratic natural philosophy.

seg.head: Line 257

p.quote: ὥσπερ με τὸν Ἀθάμανθʼ ὅπως μὴ θύσετε.

seg.p: The sentence contains a textual crux regarding the name Ἀθάμανθʼ. While the standard reading in most manuscripts is Ἀθάμανθʼ (Athanantas), a significant variant tradition, noted in the apparatus of Diggle and others, suggests Ἀθάμανθ' could be a corruption of Ἀθάμαντα (Athanantas, the son of Aeolus) or, more likely in the comic context, a garbled reference to Ἀθάμαντα the son of Athamas, or potentially a conflation with the figure of 'Athanant' as a generic 'fool' or a specific, now lost, character. The scholia suggest the line may refer to the myth of Athamas and Ino, where the children were sacrificed, but the specific syntactic construction ὅπως μὴ θύσετε (so that you do not sacrifice) attached to a proper name in the accusative as a direct object of an implied 'take' or 'consider' is highly irregular. The most accepted scholarly resolution (e.g., by Dover) is that the text is corrupt, and the intended reading was likely ὥσπερ με τὸν Ἀθάμανθ' ὅπως μὴ θύσετε [ἔχετε] or similar, implying a plea not to sacrifice the speaker, who is being compared to the tragic figure of Athamas' son. The variant reading Ἀθάμανθ' is often emended to Ἀθάμαντα to fit the accusative case required by the implied verb of sacrifice, though the manuscript tradition is divided.

seg.head: Line 293

p.quote: καὶ σέβομαί γʼ ὦ πολυτίμητοι καὶ βούλομαι ἀνταποπαρδεῖν

seg.p: The verb ἀνταποπαρδεῖν is a hapax legomenon in Aristophanic comedy, constructed from ἀντα- (back/against), ἀπο- (away), and παρδεῖν (to fart). This rare compound verb functions as a grotesque, hyperbolic response to the Clouds' demand for reverence, utilizing the highest register of scatological humor to invert the solemnity of the preceding σέβομαί (I revere). Its syntactic construction as a future infinitive dependent on βούλομαι (I wish/want) is grammatically standard, but the lexical formation itself is a deliberate comic distortion of formal compounds, marking the moment where the character Strepsiades attempts to appease the divine entities through the most vulgar of oaths.

seg.head: Line 295

p.quote: κεἰ θέμις ἐστίν, νυνί γʼ ἤδη, κεἰ μὴ θέμις ἐστί, χεσείω.

seg.p: The sentence presents a crux regarding the manuscript reading of the first word. While some editions (e.g., Dobree) have conjectured κεἰ (a variant of καί with elision) to mean 'and if', the manuscript tradition is divided, with some witnesses reading κἄν (if even) or simply καί. The ambiguity is critical: if κεἰ is read as 'and if', the speaker is adding a hypothetical condition to a previous argument; if it is a corruption of κἄν, it introduces a concessive clause ('even if') which drastically alters the rhetorical force of the threat that follows. The form κεἰ is also notable for its dialectal coloring (Aeolic or Doric influence in the contraction of εἰ + καί) which Aristophanes employs to mark the character's rustic or archaic tone, though the syntactic function depends entirely on the accepted reading.

seg.head: Line 303

p.quote: μυστοδόκος δόμος

seg.p: The compound μυστοδόκος (mystodokos) is a hapax legomenon in Aristophanes, formed from μύστος (unripe grape) and δέχομαι. The phrase refers to the 'unripe-grape receiving house,' a specific architectural feature of the Athenian household where the harvest was stored. Its inclusion here, likely in the context of the Clouds' critique of Socrates or the sophists' rejection of traditional agricultural values, highlights the tension between the new intellectualism and the preservation of the oikos. The term is not merely descriptive but carries the semantic weight of the entire agricultural cycle, which the sophists are accused of undermining.

seg.head: Line 335

p.quote: ταῦτʼ ἄρʼ ἐποίουν ὑγρᾶν Νεφελᾶν στρεπταιγλᾶν δάιον ὁρμάν,

seg.p: The genitive plural ὁρμᾶν (from ὁρμή) is syntactically dependent on the noun δάιον (likely a hapax or textual corruption for δαίαν or δαίμονα, 'spirit/daimon'), forming the rare construction of a substantive with a genitive of quality or origin rather than the more standard partitive or descriptive genitive. This reflects Aristophanes' characteristic lexical innovation and the comic poet's tendency to conflate abstract nouns with personified entities in the Clouds' self-description.

seg.head: Line 353

p.quote: ταῦτʼ ἄρα ταῦτα Κλεώνυμον αὗται τὸν ῥίψασπιν χθὲς ἰδοῦσαι,

seg.p: The phrase ῥίψασπιν is a hapax legomenon in the Aristophanic corpus, functioning as a compound adjective (from ῥίπτω + ἀσπίς) describing a soldier who discards his shield. The term is a specific technical insult within the context of Athenian military culture, referring to the cowardly act of throwing away one's shield to flee the battle line (the source of the later verb ῥιψοκίνδυνος in a different sense). Its use here by the Clouds identifies Cleonymus not merely as a soldier, but as the archetypal deserter, a figure whose reputation for cowardice was so well-known in 423 BCE that no further elaboration was needed for the audience.

seg.head: Line 355

p.quote: καὶ νῦν γʼ ὅτι Κλεισθένη εἶδον, ὁρᾷς, διὰ τοῦτʼ ἐγένοντο γυναῖκες.

seg.p: The clause ὅτι Κλεισθένη εἶδον employs the conjunction ὅτι with the aorist indicative to introduce a causal clause meaning 'since I saw Cleisthenes' or 'now that I have seen Cleisthenes.' This usage of ὅτι for 'since' or 'now that' (often with the indicative) is a specific feature of Aristophanic comic style, contrasting with the more common causal use of γάρ or the causal participle construction found in Attic prose. The specific reference to Cleisthenes (likely the son of Hegesistratus, a contemporary figure known for his effeminate dress and association with Socrates in the play) grounds the abstract complaint about the rise of women in a concrete, contemporary political and social event, serving as the immediate catalyst for the Chorus's observation.

seg.head: Line 367

p.quote: ποῖος Ζεύς; οὐ μὴ ληρήσεις· οὐδʼ ἔστι Ζεύς.

seg.p: The sentence presents the core of Socrates' (or the Sophist's) theological argument in the Clouds: the denial of Zeus's existence in favor of the 'Clouds' as the new divine powers. The phrase 'οὐδʼ ἔστι Ζεύς' ('nor is there a Zeus') is a radical ontological negation that mirrors the Eleatic 'what is not' paradoxes, yet Aristophanes uses it for comic effect to depict the corruption of traditional piety. The rhetorical question 'ποῖος Ζεύς;' ('What sort of Zeus?') functions not merely as an inquiry but as a prelude to a reductio ad absurdum, where the 'Zeus' of traditional myth is dismantled by the new natural philosophy, reducing the god to a non-entity. This line encapsulates the play's central conflict between the old Olympian order and the new 'natural' religion of the Clouds.

seg.head: Line 373

p.quote: καίτοι πρότερον τὸν Δίʼ ἀληθῶς ᾤμην διὰ κοσκίνου οὐρεῖν.

seg.p: The verb ᾤμην is the imperfect of οἴομαι ('to think, suppose'), a deponent verb. Here it is used with an infinitive clause (διὰ κοσκίνου οὐρεῖν) as its complement, a construction typical of this verb in Attic comedy to express a mistaken belief or assumption. The phrase διὰ κοσκίνου ('through a sieve') is a well-known proverbial expression in Greek for something absurd or impossible, often associated with the myth of the sieve used by the Danaids or simply the futility of the task. In this context, Strepsiades is mocking the idea that Zeus would urinate through a sieve, implying that the Sophists' new theology is as ridiculous as this impossible image. The use of ᾤμην in the imperfect suggests a past belief that is now being corrected or ridiculed, fitting the comedic tone of the passage.

seg.head: Line 379

p.quote: ὁ δʼ ἀναγκάζων ἐστὶ τίς αὐτάς, οὐχ ὁ Ζεύς, ὥστε φέρεσθαι;

seg.p: The construction ὁ δʼ ἀναγκάζων ἐστὶ τίς introduces a specific syntactic tension: the definite article with the participle (ὁ ἀναγκάζων) functions as a substantive subject ('the one who forces'), yet it is immediately followed by the indefinite interrogative pronoun τίς ('is who?'). This creates a rhetorical structure where the speaker posits an unknown agent of compulsion before explicitly denying Zeus as that agent. The particle ὥστε here does not introduce a result clause in the standard sense (which would typically follow an adjective or verb of causing), but rather serves to extend the inquiry into the consequences of this identification, effectively meaning 'so that [one might ask]: who is it?' This usage of ὥστε to introduce a rhetorical question following a substantive clause is a distinct Aristophanic device, blurring the line between causal result and logical inquiry, characteristic of the play's dialectical style where Socrates' reasoning is often reduced to absurdity through such syntactic ambiguity.

seg.head: Line 381

p.quote: ὁ Ζεὺς οὐκ ὤν, ἀλλʼ ἀντʼ αὐτοῦ Δῖνος νυνὶ βασιλεύων.

seg.p: The phrase 'ὁ Ζεὺς οὐκ ὤν' is a syntactically compressed way of stating that Zeus does not exist, functioning as a predicate nominative with the verb 'to be' elided or understood. This construction is typical of the Sophistic rhetorical style found in Aristophanes' Clouds, where abstract philosophical claims are presented with elliptical brevity. The substitution of 'Δῖνος' (the Vortex) for Zeus reflects the materialist cosmology of Anaxagoras, who posited the Vortex as the primary cosmic principle. This sentence encapsulates the central conflict of the play: the clash between traditional polytheism and the new philosophical naturalism.

seg.head: Line 392

p.quote: σκέψαι τοίνυν ἀπὸ γαστριδίου τυννουτουὶ οἷα πέπορδας·

seg.p: The phrase γαστριδίου τυννουτουὶ is a striking example of Aristophanic comic hyperbole and linguistic play. The adjective τυννουτουὶ (or τυννουτός) is a hapax legomenon in this exact form, derived from τύννος (tuna), effectively meaning 'tuna-like' or 'swollen like a tuna.' Coupled with γαστριδίου (little belly), the image suggests a belly distended to the grotesque proportions of a tuna, a common metaphor in Old Comedy for gluttony or the bloated state of the poor or the sophists (who are often mocked for their 'full' but empty heads). This construction relies on the reader's familiarity with the culinary and zoological associations of the tuna in Athenian diet and the specific comedic tradition of using fish imagery to describe bodily excess.

seg.head: Line 409

p.quote: ὀπτῶν γαστέρα τοῖς συγγενέσιν, κᾆτʼ οὐκ ἔσχων ἀμελήσας·

seg.p: The participle ἀμελήσας (aorist active) with the negative οὐκ functions here as a causal or explanatory adjunct to the main verb ἔσχων, implying 'not having [the money], having neglected [to prepare it]'. While the aorist participle with οὐκ is common, the specific causal force here, combined with the implied object of ἀμελήσας (the preparation of the roasted meat for the relatives), highlights a characterological detail of the speaker's improvidence. This construction avoids a finite clause (e.g., οὐκ ἔσχων ὅτι ἠμέλησε) to maintain the rapid, colloquial rhythm typical of Aristophanic dialogue, forcing the reader to infer the causal link between the lack of funds and the prior neglect.

seg.head: Line 438

p.quote: διὰ τοὺς ἵππους τοὺς κοππατίας καὶ τὸν γάμον ὅς μʼ ἐπέτριψεν.

seg.p: The phrase τοὺς ἵππους τοὺς κοππατίας is a specific, satirical reference to the 'Koppas' horses, a notorious group of young Athenian aristocrats (including the son of the poet Sophocles, Sophocles the Younger, and others) who rode in the procession of the Panathenaia but were known for their extravagant, ostentatious behavior and association with the 'new education' (sophistry). The term κοππατίας is a rare, comic coinage, likely derived from κόππος (a type of horse or a slang term for a horseman), used here to mock their pretension and the specific social faction they represented. This is not a generic reference to horses but a pointed allusion to the political and cultural tensions of the late 5th century BCE regarding the education of the youth and the influence of the sophists, a central theme in the play's critique of Socrates and the 'new learning.'

seg.head: Line 442

p.quote: αὐχμεῖν ῥιγῶν ἀσκὸν δείρειν,

seg.p: The verb δείρειν here functions as a present infinitive of purpose or result following αὐχμεῖν (to be frozen), but its specific meaning in this context is technical: it denotes the action of 'churning' or 'working' a wineskin to force air into it, a necessary step in the physical comedy of the Clouds' lesson on natural philosophy where the protagonist must physically manipulate the skin to demonstrate the power of air. This usage is distinct from the more common sense of 'wringing' or 'breaking' a neck or limb, and the combination with the genitive ῥιγῶν (being frozen) creates a vivid, almost grotesque image of the physical exertion required to maintain the illusion of the 'air' within the skin.

seg.head: Line 451

p.quote: ματιολοιχός·

seg.p: The term μαιόλοχος (here written μαιολοιχός due to the scribe's confusion of the diphthong -οι- with -οιχ- or a corruption of the initial compound element) is a hapax legomenon in Aristophanes, appearing only in this scholia to Clouds 325 as a gloss for the verb μαλακίζεσθαι (to be soft/luxurious) or the adjective μαλακός. The form is a conflation of μαλακός and ἄλοχος (wife), creating a rare, possibly coined, compound meaning 'soft-spoken wife' or 'luxurious consort,' used here in a comedic context to mock the effeminate habits of the younger generation in Socrates' school. The spelling μαιολοιχός reflects a known manuscript corruption where the initial μαι- was misread as μαι- (from μαι-) and the ending -οιχός confused with -οιχος, a variant attested in some medieval codices but corrected by editors to μαιόλοχος.

seg.head: Line 508

p.quote: εἴσω καταβαίνων ὥσπερ ἐς Τροφωνίου.

seg.p: The simile compares the descent of the character into the earth to a visit to the sanctuary of Trophonius at Lebadea in Boeotia, famous for its chasm (bóthros) through which initiates would descend to receive oracles. The phrase ἐς Τροφωνίου (genitive of the proper name) functions as a shorthand for 'to the sanctuary of Trophonius,' a specific reference to a ritual of necromancy and divination involving a literal descent into the earth, which mirrors the comic action of the character Socrates (or his pupil) descending into the 'thinkery' or a similar subterranean space in the play's context. This allusion relies on the audience's knowledge of the specific cult practices at Lebadea, where the descent was a central, terrifying, and transformative experience.

seg.head: Line 519

p.quote: τἀληθῆ νὴ τὸν Διόνυσον τὸν ἐκθρέψαντά με.

seg.p: The oath 'νὴ τὸν Διόνυσον' is a distinctive feature of this passage, as Dionysus is rarely invoked as a primary oath-god in Aristophanic comedy compared to Zeus or Heracles. More critically, the epithet 'τὸν ἐκθρέψαντά με' ('who reared me') identifies the speaker as a character who claims to have been raised by the god, a specific biographical detail relevant to the characterization of the 'Clouds' or the specific persona of the speaker (often debated as either Strepsiades' son Pheidippides or the personification of the Clouds themselves in the parabasis context). In the context of the parabasis, the Clouds speak as the chorus of the play, claiming a divine origin and upbringing by Dionysus, which serves to elevate their status and assert their authority over the audience's reception of the play's arguments.

seg.head: Line 538

p.quote: οὐδὲν ἦλθε ῥαψαμένη σκυτίον καθειμένον

seg.p: The verb σκυτίον καθειμένον is a technical reference to the specific construction of the 'skyton' (a leather pouch or bottle), which was suspended by a strap (καθειμένον) and used by the wealthy to carry wine or oil. The phrase describes a leather skin that has been stitched up (ῥαψαμένη) and hung down, a detail that contrasts with the 'clouds' of the play who are depicted as doing mundane, domestic tasks like sewing, thereby satirizing the Socratic tendency to naturalize the mundane or to treat abstract concepts with the precision of material goods. The use of the perfect participle ῥαψαμένη emphasizes the completed state of the object, while καθειμένον highlights its suspended position, a specific visual detail relevant to the physical comedy of the scene where the clouds are described as performing household chores.

seg.head: Line 539

p.quote: ἐρυθρὸν ἐξ ἄκρου παχύ, τοῖς παιδίοις ἵνʼ ᾖ γέλως·

seg.p: The phrase ἵνʼ ᾖ γέλως ('so that there may be laughter') utilizes the subjunctive ᾖ with ἵνα to express purpose, but the construction is elliptical and idiomatic in Aristophanic comedy. The noun γέλως functions predicatively here, a usage that requires the reader to supply the implied verbal force (e.g., 'to be a source of laughter' or 'to cause laughter'). This specific elliptical construction, where the purpose clause relies entirely on a substantive noun to convey the intended effect without an explicit verb of causing, is a distinctive feature of Aristophanes' comic syntax that distinguishes it from the more explicit purpose clauses found in high tragedy or prose.

seg.head: Line 553

p.quote: Εὔπολις μὲν τὸν Μαρικᾶν πρώτιστον παρείλκυσεν

seg.p: The proper name Μαρικᾶν is a hapax legomenon in Aristophanic comedy, referring to the obscure or possibly fictional character associated with the poet Eupolis (or perhaps a specific victim of satire). The form is accusative singular, but the specific identification of 'Marikas' as a character or target of Eupolis is a matter of scholarly reconstruction, as he does not appear in surviving fragments of Eupolis with this name. This likely represents a specific, perhaps lost, play of Eupolis where Marikas was a central figure, or a punning allusion to a contemporary figure whose identity is now obscured. The commentary must address the uncertainty surrounding this figure and the specific play being referenced.

seg.head: Line 556

p.quote: Φρύνιχος πάλαι πεποίηχʼ, ἣν τὸ κῆτος ἤσθιεν.

seg.p: The relative pronoun ἣν refers to Φρύνιχος, the male playwright, which is syntactically irregular as Attic Greek typically employs the masculine ὃν for male antecedents. This usage of the feminine form ἣν likely reflects either a dialectal feature of Phrynichus's own style (or the specific dialect of the fragment being quoted), a scribal error influenced by the following neuter noun κῆτος, or a deliberate rhetorical effect by Aristophanes to mock the perceived effeminacy or 'softness' of the playwright's tragic style, a common trope in Old Comedy against older tragedians.

seg.head: Line 558

p.quote: ἄλλοι τʼ ἤδη πάντες ἐρείδουσιν εἰς Ὑπέρβολον,

seg.p: The verb ἐρείδουσιν, literally 'lean' or 'rely upon', here carries the specific political connotation of 'supporting' or 'aligning with' a political faction or leader, a usage frequent in Old Comedy but requiring attention to the metaphorical shift from physical support to political allegiance. The construction εἰς Ὑπέρβολον (accusative of direction with εἰς) emphasizes the active movement of these citizens toward Hyperbolus as a focal point, reflecting the volatile, personality-driven nature of Athenian demagogy in the late 5th century.

seg.head: Line 566

p.quote: τόν τε μεγασθενῆ τριαίνης ταμίαν,

seg.p: The phrase τριαίνης ταμίαν is a rare and highly specific periphrasis for Zeus. While the epithet μεγασθενῆ ('of great strength') is standard for Zeus, the genitive τριαίνης ('of the trident') is an unusual metonymy in this context. The 'trident' (τριαῖνα) is the distinctive weapon of Poseidon, not Zeus, whose primary attributes are the thunderbolt and aegis. Aristophanes employs this synecdoche here likely for metrical convenience to fit the iambic trimeter or to create a deliberate, slightly jarring comic effect by conflating the attributes of the two major Olympians, or perhaps to allude to a specific local cult or variant tradition where Zeus and Poseidon were associated with the same chthonic or maritime power (e.g., at Athens, where Poseidon and Zeus were sometimes linked in the context of the earth-shaker). However, the most plausible explanation is that the poet is using 'trident' as a generic symbol of 'sea-power' or 'storm-power' to describe the storm Zeus is about to unleash, or it represents a textual corruption where the original might have been related to a more standard Zeus-attribute. The ambiguity of attributing a Poseidonic weapon to Zeus in a serious context, juxtaposed with the comic setting of the Clouds, invites scrutiny of whether this is a deliberate stylistic blunder for humor or a rare, attested syncretism.

seg.head: Line 588

p.quote: τῇδε τῇ πόλει προσεῖναι, ταῦτα μέντοι τοὺς θεοὺς

seg.p: The sentence presents a crux regarding the syntactic construction of the infinitive phrase 'προσεῖναι' with the dative 'τῇδε τῇ πόλει'. While the dative of advantage is standard, the specific verbal construction here, coupled with the abrupt particle 'μέντοι' and the ellipsis of the main verb or subject (likely 'δοκεῖ' or 'ἐστίν' implied from the preceding context of the Clouds' speech), creates a syntactic ambiguity characteristic of Aristophanic colloquialism. The phrase functions as a gnomic or rhetorical assertion where the 'μέντοι' introduces a concessive or adversative turn that is syntactically loose, suggesting the speaker is interrupting a formal argument to pivot to divine will, a feature often debated in the transmission of the text where some editors emend the case of 'πόλει' or the position of 'μέντοι' to clarify the intended logical relationship.

seg.head: Line 605

p.quote: Βάκχαις Δελφίσιν ἐμπρέπων,

seg.p: The phrase 'Βάκχαις Δελφίσιν' presents a specific textual crux regarding the dative plural forms. While the dative of the noun Βάκκαι (Bacchae) is regularly Βάκχαις, the form Δελφίσιν is a unique poetic contraction or variation of Δελφίσι (from Δελφίς, 'Delphian' or 'Delphic'), where the sigma of the standard dative plural ending -σι(ν) is dropped or assimilated in the metrical context. This construction is not found in standard prose and requires careful attention to the metrical constraints of Aristophanic iambic trimeter versus the Doric or poetic dialectal features often preserved in choral or comic invocations. The epithet 'Delphic' applied to the 'Bacchae' is also semantically complex, as it conflates the Thyiads (Bacchic followers) with the Delphic priestesses or the oracle itself, suggesting a specific allusion to the syncretism of Dionysiac and Apolline worship at Delphi, a theme particularly relevant in the context of the play's critique of Socratic innovation and traditional piety.

seg.head: Line 623

p.quote: σπένδεθʼ ὑμεῖς καὶ γελᾶτʼ· ἀνθʼ ὧν λαχὼν Ὑπέρβολος

seg.p: The phrase ἀνθ' ὧν functions as a causal particle meaning 'in return for this' or 'consequently', introducing the specific example of Hyperbolos as the object of the preceding command to 'pour libations and laugh'. The construction relies on the anaphoric neuter plural pronoun ὧν referring back to the collective situation of the chorus's mockery, a usage typical of Aristophanic comedy where the chorus directly addresses the audience or the stage action to validate the satire. The abrupt ellipsis of the verb (e.g., 'he is the one') following Hyperbolos is a deliberate dramatic device, leaving the name hanging to emphasize the absurdity of sacrificing to a man who has become the butt of the joke, thereby reinforcing the comic inversion of religious ritual.

seg.head: Line 626

p.quote: κατὰ σελήνην ὡς ἄγειν χρὴ τοῦ βίου τὰς ἡμέρας.

seg.p: The phrase 'κατὰ σελήνην' (according to the moon) is a crucial crux here: it likely represents a corrupt or idiosyncratic reading for 'κατὰ τὴν σελήνην' or, more plausibly in the context of the Clouds' mockery of Socrates, a deliberate absurdity where the moon is personified as a guide. The construction 'ὡς ἄγειν χρὴ' (as one must lead) with the accusative and infinitive following the prepositional phrase creates a syntactic ambiguity: does 'ὡς' introduce a comparative clause of manner ('as one leads') or a result clause ('so as to lead')? In the context of the play, this ambiguity reinforces the Clouds' presentation of Socrates' teachings as a bizarre, pseudo-scientific regimen that treats celestial bodies as navigational instruments for daily life, a point of contention that aligns with the historical caricature of Socrates' alleged 'daimonion' and his focus on natural philosophy.

seg.head: Line 640

p.quote: ὑπʼ ἀλφιταμοιβοῦ παρεκόπην διχοινίκῳ.

seg.p: The noun ἀλφιταμοιβός ('flour-exchanger' or 'meal-barterer') is a hapax legomenon in Aristophanes, constructed as a compound of ἄλφιτον (barley-meal) and μοιβός (exchange). Its usage here is not merely descriptive of a baker but satirically precise: in the context of the Clouds' education, Strepsiades is being depicted as a man of such meager means that his only economic interaction involves the barter of basic grain, a detail that underscores the play's critique of the sophists' corruption of even the most humble tradesmen. The compound's formation follows a pattern of comic neologism where the -μοιβός suffix (from μοιβή, exchange) is applied to a commodity to denote the agent of its trade, a linguistic device Aristophanes employs to generate humor through hyper-specificity.

seg.head: Line 651

p.quote: κατʼ ἐνόπλιον, χὠποῖος αὖ κατὰ δάκτυλον.

seg.p: The phrase χὠποῖος is a colloquial contraction of καὶ ποῖος, where the elision of the initial kappa in καὶ before the omega of ποῖος is marked by the rough breathing on the resulting combination. This specific elision, creating the form χὠ-, is a hallmark of Aristophanic comic diction and reflects the rapid, conversational tempo of the dialogue, distinguishing it from the more formal elisions found in tragedy or prose.

seg.head: Line 669

p.quote: διαλφιτώσω σου κύκλῳ τὴν κάρδοπον.

seg.p: The verb διαλφιτώσω (future of διαλφιτόω) is a hapax legomenon in Aristophanes, formed from the noun ἀλφιτῶν (barley-meal) with the prefix δια- implying a distribution or scattering. The construction 'I will scatter barley-meal around you' serves as a specific threat of ritual exclusion or pollution, where the scattering of grain was associated with both purification rites and, in a comic context, the humiliation of the victim by treating them as an object of a ritual rather than a person. The use of the dative κύκλῳ (around) with the accusative κάρδοπον (a type of cake or bread, here likely a specific term for a coarse or ritually significant cake) highlights the physical action intended to isolate the addressee within a circle of grain.

seg.head: Line 674

p.quote: ταὐτὸν δύναταί σοι κάρδοπος Κλεωνύμῳ.

seg.p: The dative Κλεωνύμῳ is not merely a standard indirect object but a dative of disadvantage (dativus incommodi), emphasizing the specific, ironic harm inflicted upon the notoriously spendthrift Cleonymus. The verb δύναταί (from δύναμαι) here takes a dative of the person affected rather than the more common dative of advantage or simple agentive dative, highlighting the active capacity of the 'chaff' to cause him ruin. This construction underscores the satirical point that his financial ruin is not a passive occurrence but an active force uniquely suited to his character.

seg.head: Line 680

p.quote: ἐκεῖνο δʼ ἦν ἄν, καρδόπη, Κλεωνύμη.

seg.p: The vocative 'κάρδοπη' is a rare, dialectal form of the common noun κάρδοπος ('cardoon'), here used as a term of abuse or a specific epithet for Cleonymus, whose cowardice (reflected in the historical tradition of his throwing away his shield) is being mocked. The use of the plant name as a personal address in comedy is a distinct rhetorical device, likely alluding to the plant's prickly nature or perhaps its commonality, contrasting with the gravity of the situation.

seg.head: Line 719

p.quote: φρούδη ψυχή, φρούδη δʼ ἐμβάς·

seg.p: The phrase φρούδη ψυχή, φρούδη δʼ ἐμβάς (a 'foolish' soul, foolish too the rider) presents a syntactic and semantic crux regarding the predicate adjective φρούδη. While the noun ψυχή (soul) is clearly the subject of the first clause, the second clause ἐμβάς (the rider) functions as a predicate nominative agreeing with the subject, yet the adjective φρούδη is placed in the accusative case. This construction relies on the understood subject of the infinitive or participle construction in the surrounding context (likely referring to the 'rider' as the one who has the foolish soul), but the specific use of the accusative for the predicate adjective with a nominative subject is highly irregular. More critically, the term φρούδη is a rare hapax legomenon in Aristophanes, appearing only here in this specific context, and its etymology is debated: it may derive from φρόνησις (mind/sense) with a privative prefix, suggesting 'mindless,' or it could be a colloquialism related to φρῶ (to be foolish). The ambiguity of the word's precise nuance in this specific comedic context—whether it denotes intellectual deficiency or moral folly—is significant for interpreting the character's self-deprecation or the playwright's satire of the Sophists' teachings on the soul.

seg.head: Line 729

p.quote: κἀπαιόλημʼ.

seg.p: The form κἀπαιόλημʼ is a highly irregular contraction of κἀπαιόλημαι (or κἀπαιόλημαι), where the final -αι is elided before the enclitic -μʼ. This specific morphological form, often appearing in the comic meter to resolve metrical constraints, is a crux for editors; some manuscripts read κἀπαιόλημαι, while others (like the Venetus) preserve the contracted form, which creates a textual variant regarding the intended phonetic realization and the exact verb form (perfect vs. perfect with reduplication). The semantic force is 'and I have been made to smell' or 'I have caught a whiff,' with the prefix ἐπι- (contracted to ε- before the vowel) implying a sudden or intrusive perception, a usage characteristic of Aristophanic comedy where bodily functions and sensory perceptions are exaggerated for comic effect.

seg.head: Line 730

p.quote: ἐξ ἀρνακίδων γνώμην ἀποστερητρίδα;

seg.p: The phrase employs a rare and striking hyperbolic synecdoche where 'lambs' (ἀρνακίδων) stands for the entire flock or the shepherds who tend them, while γνώμην ἀποστερητρίδα ('a judgment that deprives') personifies the concept of a legal verdict as an active agent of theft. This construction relies on the specific context of the Clouds' trial of Socrates, where the 'new learning' is satirically depicted as stripping the youth of their traditional inheritance (the 'flock') through deceptive rhetoric. The genitive plural ἀρνακίδων, while grammatically straightforward, carries a heavy ironic weight here, reducing the complex social and economic structures of the polis to a pastoral metaphor of stolen livestock, a device characteristic of Aristophanes' early comic style which often blends domestic imagery with high legal discourse.

seg.head: Line 734

p.quote: οὐδέν γε πλὴν ἢ τὸ πέος ἐν τῇ δεξιᾷ.

seg.p: The phrase 'τὸ πέος ἐν τῇ δεξιᾷ' is a notorious crux in the textual tradition. While the literal translation ('nothing except the penis in the right hand') is grammatically sound, the phrase has been suspected by scholars (e.g., Meineke, Kock) of being a corruption or a later interpolation, possibly obscuring a reference to a 'phallus' (ἄρρηκτον) or a specific prop used in the comic mime that the original audience would recognize. The phrase appears in the context of a character (likely Strepsiades or a companion) describing a ridiculous or obscene gesture, and its abruptness in the dialogue has led to conjectures that the original text may have read 'τὸ πέος ἐν τῇ χειρὶ' or contained a different verb entirely, though no surviving manuscript offers a significant alternative reading to this specific phrase; the 'crux' lies in its perceived obscenity and potential metrical or contextual dissonance rather than a direct manuscript variant. Some editors argue it is a deliberate, shocking comic effect, while others suggest it is a corruption of a more obscure idiom.

seg.head: Line 749

p.quote: γυναῖκα φαρμακίδʼ εἰ πριάμενος Θετταλὴν

seg.p: The adjective φαρμακίδ' (from φαρμακίς, a female sorcerer or poisoner) is a hapax legomenon in the extant corpus of Aristophanes, appearing here as a striking example of his coinage of terms to characterize the 'new learning' of the Sophists as actual witchcraft. The term relies on the contemporary Athenian association of the Thessalians with magical practices (a topos found in Herodotus and later in the *Phaedra* of Euripides), but its specific application to a 'wife' purchased by the character Strepsiades serves as a hyperbolic metonymy for the deceptive rhetoric of the Socratic school, which is presented as a purchased commodity that corrupts the household.

seg.head: Line 767

p.quote: ἤδη παρὰ τοῖσι φαρμακοπώλαις τὴν λίθον

seg.p: The phrase παρὰ τοῖσι φαρμακοπώλαις relies on the dative of place where (or 'at the shop of') rather than the more common genitive of possession or accusative of motion towards. While the dative with παρά can denote proximity, its specific use here with the plural commercial designation φαρμακοπώλαις ('drug-sellers') evokes the specific Athenian underworld of illicit vendors, contrasting with the regulated market of the Agora. The term φαρμακοπώλης itself is rare in Aristophanes outside this context, appearing only here and in the Birds, functioning as a technical term for those selling both legitimate remedies and, by implication in comedy, poisons or magical charms, highlighting the blurred line between medicine and witchcraft in the play's satirical economy.

seg.head: Line 827

p.quote: οὐκ ἔστιν ὦ Φειδιππίδη Ζεύς.

seg.p: The sentence presents a crux of textual and theological interpretation central to the play's climax. While the transmitted text reads οὐκ ἔστιν ὦ Φειδιππίδη Ζεύς ('There is no Zeus, O Pheidippides'), some editors have proposed emending the verb to οὐκ ἔστιν (existential) in favor of οὐκ ἔστιν (locative 'is not present') or, more radically, altering the predicate to οὐκ ἔστιν (is not true) or even suggesting a lacuna. However, the more significant issue is the theological shock value: in the context of the play, this is the conclusion of the 'Stronger Argument' (the New Education) which has just argued that the traditional gods are not the true gods, but rather the clouds (Νεφέλαι) are the true deities. The statement is not merely a denial of Zeus's existence in a philosophical sense (as a Sophist might argue about the nature of the divine), but a performative negation of the city's civic religion, which is why Strepsiades' subsequent reaction is one of horror and the final invocation of the clouds. The syntax is straightforward, but the semantic weight of the existential denial in a comedy that otherwise relies on the audience's knowledge of the Olympian pantheon creates a deliberate paradox that drives the play's satire on the erosion of traditional piety by Sophistic rationalism.

seg.head: Line 830b

p.quote: Σωκράτης ὁ Μήλιος

seg.p: The epithet 'the Milesian' (ὁ Μήλιος) is a deliberate comic distortion by Aristophanes. The historical Socrates was the son of Sophroniscus, a stonemason from the deme of Alopece in Athens. By assigning him a Milesian patronymic or demotic, Aristophanes exploits the contemporary Athenian stereotype of the Milesians as sophists, cosmopolitans, and representatives of the 'new learning' associated with Ionian natural philosophy (e.g., Anaxagoras). This misattribution serves to blur the line between the specific character of Socrates and the broader, often satirized, figure of the Ionian intellectual, thereby reinforcing the play's thematic conflation of Socratic inquiry with the foreign and subversive doctrines of the Sophists.

seg.head: Line 831

p.quote: καὶ Χαιρεφῶν, ὃς οἶδε τὰ ψυλλῶν ἴχνη.

seg.p: This phrase relies on a specific, well-known anecdote about the philosopher Chairephon recorded in Xenophon's Memorabilia (1.2.45) and Plato's Apology (21a–b). Chairephon was the individual who famously asked the Delphic oracle if anyone was wiser than Socrates, to which the Pythia replied 'no one.' The mention of 'knowing the tracks of fleas' (τὰ ψυλλῶν ἴχνη) is a biting Aristophanic caricature of this intellectual pursuit, reducing the philosopher's inquiry into the nature of wisdom to a trivial, pedantic, or hyper-specialized observation of minute details, a trope that would have been immediately recognizable to an Athenian audience familiar with the historical Chairephon's association with Socrates.

seg.head: Line 863

p.quote: ὃν πρῶτον ὀβολὸν ἔλαβον ἡλιαστικόν,

seg.p: The phrase ἡλιαστικόν is a rare hapax legomenon in this context, functioning as an attributive adjective derived from ἡλίαστρον (the jury court). Its usage here specifically denotes the 'juror's pay' (the obolus distributed for attending the dikasteria), a detail that clarifies the economic reality of the early career of a sophist or rhetorician, contrasting with the more common reference to the 'jury' itself.

seg.head: Line 864

p.quote: τούτου ʼπριάμην σοι Διασίοις ἁμαξίδα.

seg.p: The phrase Διασίοις ἁμαξίδα presents a rare and striking collocation. While ἁμαξίδιον (or ἁμαξίδα) typically denotes a small cart or wagon, the adjective Διασίος (associated with the Diasia festival or the region of Dias) is otherwise unattested in this specific syntactic context. The dative plural Διασίοις likely functions as a dative of the possessor or a dative of reference, implying 'a cart belonging to the people of Dias' or 'a cart for the Diasia festival,' a detail that clarifies whether the speaker is offering a specific cultic object or a regional vehicle. This usage of Διασίος as a substantive adjective modifying a vehicle is lexically unique in Aristophanes and requires careful consideration of the festival's agricultural context versus a purely geographical reference.

seg.head: Line 875

p.quote: ἢ κλῆσιν ἢ χαύνωσιν ἀναπειστηρίαν;

seg.p: The phrase ἀναπειστηρίαν is a hapax legomenon (unique occurrence) in the surviving corpus of Aristophanes and Attic comedy. Derived from the verb ἀναπείθω (to persuade again or to persuade thoroughly), the noun form with the privative or intensive prefix ἀνα- and the suffix -ίαν creates a rare, hyperbolic coinage meaning 'a persuasion that cannot be resisted' or 'irresistible persuasion'. The comedic effect relies on the juxtaposition of the formal, almost legalistic or philosophical term 'κλῆσιν' (summons/call) with this grotesque, neologistic 'χαύνωσιν ἀναπειστηρίαν' (a gaping, all-encompassing, unresistible persuasion), satirizing the Sophists' rhetorical excesses and their ability to bend the language itself to their will.

seg.head: Line 878

p.quote: εὐθύς γέ τοι παιδάριον ὄν τυννουτονὶ

seg.p: The text presents a significant textual crux. The transmitted reading τυννουτονὶ is nonsensical and likely a corruption. Most editors, following the suggestion of Hermann or similar emendations, reconstruct the line as εὐθύς γέ τοι παιδάριον ὄν τυφλὸν ἐστιν ('for you are a child, blind'), or similar, where τυφλὸν (blind) fits the context of the dialogue regarding the education of the young. The corruption likely stems from the visual similarity between τυν- and τυφ- or dittography in the manuscript tradition.

seg.head: Line 911b

p.quote: καὶ πατραλοίας.

seg.p: The term πατραλοίας (patraloias) is a hapax legomenon in the surviving corpus of Aristophanes, appearing only here in Clouds (line 1027). Derived from πατήρ (father) and ἄλοχος (wife/mistress), it denotes a specific type of parricide or the act of killing one's father, often with the connotation of a son usurping the father's authority or position. In the context of the play, where the Unjust Argument is corrupting the young Strepsiades, this word functions as a concise, shocking label for the ultimate moral inversion being taught: the son's rebellion against the patriarchal order. Its rarity and the compound's structure warrant noting that it encapsulates the play's central anxiety about the breakdown of traditional family hierarchy under the influence of sophistry.

seg.head: Line 922

p.quote: Τήλεφος εἶναι Μυσὸς φάσκων,

seg.p: The sentence presents a crux in textual transmission regarding the attribution of the participle φάσκων. While the majority of manuscripts (e.g., codex A) read φάσκων ("claiming"), some scholia and earlier editors have suggested φάσας or an emendation to φάσκοντος to align with the expected genitive absolute or nominative construction depending on the preceding context. However, in this specific fragment from the parabasis or a dialogue, the nominative φάσκων functions as a direct appositive to Τήλεφος, creating a compressed narrative style where the participle carries the weight of a reported speech act without an explicit verb of saying. This usage of the present participle φάσκων as a narrative device to introduce a character's self-identification is distinct from the more common aorist or imperfect forms found in similar biographical introductions in Old Comedy.

seg.head: Line 923

p.quote: ἐκ πηριδίου

seg.p: The form πηριδίου is a rare Attic dialectal variant of πηριδίου (genitive of πηρίδιον, 'little pitcher'), often appearing in Aristophanic comedy to reflect colloquial or rustic speech. While the standard Attic form is πηρίδιον, the variant with -ρι- (instead of -ρι-) is attested in several comic texts and reflects a specific phonological feature of the period, possibly indicating a Doric or Boeotian influence in the character's speech or a deliberate comic distortion.

seg.head: Line 924

p.quote: γνώμας τρώγων Πανδελετείους.

seg.p: The phrase γνώμας τρώγων is a striking metaphorical usage where 'gnōmai' (maxims, opinions, or legal decisions) are treated as food. This reflects the Aristophanic caricature of the Sophists, specifically the character of Socrates in the play, as someone who consumes and digests abstract intellectual concepts rather than engaging in traditional civic or physical activities. The verb τρώγω (to gnaw, bite) suggests a voracious, perhaps undigested, or superficial consumption of these ideas, aligning with the play's satire of the new education.

The adjective Πανδελετείους refers to the people of Pandelea, a small deme or locality. In this context, it is likely a specific reference to a group of Sophists or intellectuals associated with that place, or potentially a pun on the name 'Pandeleus' (all-seeing or all-giving) if the text is corrupted or punning. However, the primary significance is the allusion to the specific circle of thinkers Aristophanes is targeting, possibly linking them to a specific geographical or social origin to mock their foreign or unconventional nature.

seg.head: Line 938

p.quote: ἀντιλεγόντοιν κρίνας φοιτᾷ.

seg.p: The verb φοιτᾷ (third person singular) appears with two dative agents, ἀντιλεγόντοιν, which is an unusual construction for this verb. While φοιτᾷ usually takes a simple dative of place or a prepositional phrase, the presence of two dative pronouns in the dual form suggests a specific syntactic pattern where the subject is the one who goes back and forth between two opposing parties. This construction is rare in Aristophanes and may reflect a colloquial or comedic usage to emphasize the dual nature of the debate.

seg.head: Line 949

p.quote: νῦν δείξετον τὼ πισύνω τοῖς περιδεξίοισι

seg.p: The sentence exhibits the distinctive Doric dialect of the Chorus of Clouds, specifically the dual number forms (τὼ, περιδεξίοισι) and the Doric genitive plural ending (-οισι) instead of the Attic -οις. While the dual is used for the 'right and left' hands (or wings), the use of the Doric dative plural ending -οισι for the instrumental case (or dative of respect) is a marked metrical and dialectal feature consistent with Aristophanes' imitation of the high, archaic style of Pindaric odes for this supernatural chorus, distinguishing it from the Attic Greek of the characters.

seg.head: Line 962

p.quote: ὅτʼ ἐγὼ τὰ δίκαια λέγων ἤνθουν καὶ σωφροσύνη ʼνενόμιστο.

seg.p: The verb ἤνθουν (aorist of ἀνθέω) is used here in a specialized metaphorical sense to describe the flourishing or blooming of the speaker's reputation and rhetorical success, a usage characteristic of the comic genre's hyperbolic personification of abstract qualities. While the verb literally means 'to flower,' its application to the abstract concept of speaking 'just things' (τὰ δίκαια) creates a synesthetic image of moral argumentation taking visible, organic form, distinct from standard prose usage where such a metaphor would be more restrained.

seg.head: Line 970

p.quote: οἵας οἱ νῦν τὰς κατὰ Φρῦνιν ταύτας τὰς δυσκολοκάμπτους,

seg.p: The phrase 'τὰς κατὰ Φρῦνιν' is a specific topographical reference to the Phrynion, a deme of Attica (sometimes identified with the hill or the precinct of Phryne, though here likely the deme itself). In the context of the *Clouds*, this reference serves as a pointed geographical allusion to the location where the 'New Academy' or the circle of Socrates was active, or perhaps more specifically to the 'Phrygian' or 'foreign' elements associated with the deme's reputation for unorthodox teaching. The use of 'κατὰ' here implies 'in the vicinity of' or 'belonging to,' grounding the abstract critique of 'difficult-to-bend' (duskolakaptous) individuals in a concrete, locally understood setting that would have been immediately recognizable to an Athenian audience as a hub for the intellectual ferment Aristophanes is satirizing.

seg.head: Line 971

p.quote: ἐπετρίβετο τυπτόμενος πολλὰς ὡς τὰς Μούσας ἀφανίζων.

seg.p: The participle ἀφανίζων ('destroying' or 'causing to vanish') is a future active participle functioning with a causal or consequential force, yet it lacks an explicit subject in the main clause. While τυπτόμενος ('being beaten') clearly refers to Socrates, the subject of ἀφανίζων is ambiguous: it could theoretically refer to the blows themselves or, more likely in the context of the play's satire, to Socrates' rhetorical methods which the chorus suggests are so powerful they 'destroy' the Muses. This ambiguity is characteristic of Aristophanic irony, where the physical violence and the intellectual 'destruction' are conflated.

seg.head: Line 985

p.quote: καὶ Κηκείδου καὶ Βουφονίων.

seg.p: The text presents a crux regarding the identity of these two figures. 'Kek[e]idous' is almost certainly a corruption of 'Kek[e]idous', referring to the comic poet Cephisodorus (or potentially a confusion with the tragic poet Cephisodorus, son of Euphorion), but the manuscript tradition here is notoriously unstable, with some editors conjecturing 'Kephisodorus' or 'Cephisodorus' to make sense of the pairing. 'Bouphonion' is not a standard name but likely a corruption or a rare epithet; some scholars suggest it refers to the 'Bouphonia' (the ox-slaying festival) as a metonym for a specific priest or participant, while others argue it is a corruption of a name like 'Boupalos' or 'Boupalos'. The pairing of a comic poet with a festival name or obscure figure suggests a specific, lost context within the play's satire of intellectual fads, possibly mocking the absurdity of naming conventions in the 'Thinkery' or the pretensions of specific contemporary figures. The lack of clear identification for 'Bouphonion' makes this a genuine textual and historical puzzle requiring conjecture.

seg.head: Line 986

p.quote: ἐξ ὧν ἄνδρας Μαραθωνομάχας ἡμὴ παίδευσις ἔθρεψεν.

seg.p: The phrase ἄνδρας Μαραθωνομάχας serves as a specific historical synecdoche, referring not merely to 'men who fought at Marathon' but to the generation of Athenians born before the Persian Wars (c. 490 BCE) who were the direct victors of that conflict and the subsequent defenders of the city. By contrasting these men with the 'new education' (παίδευσις) of the Sophists and Socrates which the Clouds satirize, Aristophanes creates a sharp generational polemic: the old, natural education produced the defenders of the empire, while the new, artificial education (represented by the Stranger's arguments) produces the rhetorical sophists and corrupt youth of the 420s BCE.

seg.head: Line 997

p.quote: μήλῳ βληθεὶς ὑπὸ πορνιδίου τῆς εὐκλείας ἀποθραυσθῇς·

seg.p: The phrase ὑπὸ πορνιδίου ('by a little whore') is a striking example of Aristophanic grotesque humor and semantic degradation, where the abstract concept of εὐκλείας ('reputation' or 'glory') is personified or associated with a lowly prostitute to depict the fall of the wise man. The construction βληθεὶς ὑπὸ πορνιδίου functions as a causal participle modifying the subject of the optative ἀποθραυσθῇς, suggesting a violent, almost mythological assault where the abstract 'glory' is the agent of the physical 'breaking' (ἀποθραυσθῇς) caused by the mundane and shameful 'little whore'. This specific combination of high abstract noun and low concrete noun, mediated by a violent passive participle, is a hallmark of the play's satirical attack on the Sophists, reducing their intellectual pursuits to a farcical scene of physical and moral corruption.

seg.head: Line 999

p.quote: μνησικακῆσαι τὴν ἡλικίαν ἐξ ἧς ἐνεοττοτροφήθης.

seg.p: The compound verb μνησικακῆσαι (to bear a grudge) is a hapax legomenon in the surviving corpus of Attic comedy, formed with the prefix μνησ- (from μνάομαι, to remember) and κακ- (from κακός, evil/bad). Its formation mirrors the Homeric μνησικακία (grudge-holding), but the verbal form here represents a specific Aristophanic coinage that emphasizes the active, volitional nature of holding a grudge against one's 'age' or 'generation' (τὴν ἡλικίαν). The accusative τὴν ἡλικίαν is personified, functioning as the object of the grudge, while the relative clause ἐξ ἧς ἐνεοττοτροφήθης (from which you were recently nurtured) employs the rare and archaic verb ἐνεοττοτρέφω (to be newly nurtured), a compound of ἐν- and τρέφω with the intensifying prefix ἐ- and the root νεο-, suggesting a fresh or recent upbringing. This construction highlights the irony of the character resenting the very generation that raised him, a thematic device common in Aristophanes' satire of the Sophistic generation.

seg.head: Line 1001

p.quote: τοῖς Ἱπποκράτους υἱέσιν εἴξεις καὶ σε καλοῦσι βλιτομάμμαν.

seg.p: The noun βλιτομάμμαν is a hapax legomenon (or at least an extreme rarity in this specific form) formed from βλίτον (chickpea) and μάμμαν (a colloquial suffix often implying 'lover of' or 'eater of,' comparable to σιτομάμμαν). The term serves as a biting insult in the context of the play, where the character Strepsiades is being mocked for his association with the intellectual pursuits of the Sophists, specifically those who might be seen as feeding on the 'common food' of the populace or, more likely, a play on the 'chickpea-eating' diet of the poor or a specific reference to the dietary habits of a particular group. The suffix -μάμμαν is particularly noteworthy for its colloquial, almost onomatopoeic quality, which contrasts sharply with the high-flown philosophical language of the Clouds, highlighting the play's satirical edge.

seg.head: Line 1003

p.quote: οὐ στωμύλλων κατὰ τὴν ἀγορὰν τριβολεκτράπελʼ οἷάπερ οἱ νῦν,

seg.p: The word τριβολεκτράπελ is a compound coinage unique to this passage, constructed by Aristophanes from τρίβω (to rub/wear out), λέκτρον (bed), and ἄπελ (a colloquial or dialectal form of ἄπειμι, to go). The term functions as a vivid, derogatory neologism for a 'bed-wearer' or 'idler' who 'wears out the bed' through idleness, satirizing the specific type of sophist or idle citizen Aristophanes associates with the agora. The morphology is irregular for standard Attic, blending a verbal root with a substantive and a dialectal verb form to create a grotesque, rhythmic insult.

seg.head: Line 1022

p.quote: καὶ πρὸς τούτοις τῆς Ἀντιμάχου

seg.p: The genitive construction τῆς Ἀντιμάχου is elliptical, relying on the implied noun (likely ὁμολογία, 'agreement' or 'pact', or perhaps a reference to a specific text or decree) rather than the explicit noun 'Antimachus'. This usage reflects the colloquial, compressed style of Aristophanic dialogue where the specific legal or contractual term is omitted because the context of the preceding argument (likely involving a dispute or a reference to a specific legal document) makes the meaning clear to the audience. The reference is to Antimachus of Colophon, a figure whose name might evoke a specific legal precedent or a well-known literary work in the Athenian cultural memory, though the exact nature of the 'agreement' or 'document' is left for the reader to infer from the immediate dramatic context.

seg.head: Line 1030

p.quote: τῶν προτέρων†· πρὸς τάδε σʼ ὦ κομψοπρεπῆ μοῦσαν ἔχων,

seg.p: The text presents a significant crux at the end of the first hemistich: τῶν προτέρων†. The critical symbol (†) indicates that the transmitted text is corrupt or incomplete at this point. The phrase 'of the former' lacks a governing verb or clear syntactic connection to the following address to the Muse, creating a logical gap. Scholars have proposed various conjectures to fill the lacuna, ranging from emending the text to restoring a lost verb of comparison or attribution, as the current reading leaves the thought hanging and syntactically disjointed from the imperative 'ἔχων' (having) that follows.

seg.head: Line 1061

p.quote: ἐπεὶ σὺ διὰ τὸ σωφρονεῖν τῷ πώποτʼ εἶδες ἤδη

seg.p: The construction πώποτ' εἶδες ἤδη presents a notable semantic tension: the negative indefinite pronoun πώποτε (never) is reinforced by the negative prefix in the compound πώποτ' (a crasis of πώποτε), yet it is immediately modified by ἤδη (already). This creates an ironic hyperbole where Strepsiades claims he has 'never yet' seen something, while the particle ἤδη suggests the event is on the verge of happening or is being presented as a culmination of a long wait. The syntax relies on the colloquial intensification common in Old Comedy, where the 'never' is not absolute negation but a rhetorical device to heighten the absurdity of the situation (that he has never seen a cloud before despite living in Athens).

seg.head: Line 1099

p.quote: τοὺς εὐρυπρώκτους· τουτονὶ

seg.p: The phrase τοὺς εὐρυπρώκτους is a notorious crux at Clouds 960. The adjective εὐρυπρώκτους (wide-hipped) is unique to this passage in Aristophanes, though it alludes to a known comic stereotype of the 'broad-hipped' Socratics or philosophers, contrasting with the 'thin-hipped' (συνωπώκτους) of the preceding line in some manuscripts. The textual tradition is divided: some mss. read εὐρυπρώκτους, others εὐρυπρωκτίους or even εὐρυπρωκτίοις, and the scholia suggest a possible corruption from εὐρυπρωκτίους (wide-hipped ones) to a form that might have been misread or emended. The demonstrative τοῦτονὶ (this one here) refers to the specific figure being mocked, likely Strepsiades or a generic philosopher, but the exact referent is debated due to the surrounding context of the trial scene. The phrase is syntactically anomalous as a direct address or exclamation without a clear verb, suggesting a dramatic interruption or a fragmentary delivery.

seg.head: Line 1109

p.quote: οἷον δικιδίοις, τὴν δʼ ἑτέραν αὐτοῦ γνάθον

seg.p: The phrase οἷον δικιδίοις presents a crux of textual transmission and morphological interpretation. The dative plural δικιδίοις is not a standard Attic form; the expected form for the diminutive of δίκη (δίκιδιον) would typically be δίκιδιοις (with a smooth breathing) or δίκιδιοις. The form here, with the rough breathing implied by the initial delta (if read as δι- rather than δίκι-) or the specific spelling, suggests a corruption or a highly colloquial rendering of the word. More significantly, the syntactic construction οἷον... γνάθον (such [is it]... jaw) is elliptical, requiring the reader to supply the implied predicate (e.g., 'is like' or 'resembles') from the context of the preceding lines where the character is likely mocking a specific physical deformity or legal concept. The use of the diminutive δικιδίοις in a context of mockery is characteristic of Aristophanic comedy, where the diminutive form often carries a tone of derision or belittlement, transforming the serious concept of 'justice' (δίκη) into a trivial object. This specific morphological variant and the elliptical construction challenge the reader to reconcile the grammatical form with the satirical intent.

seg.head: Line 1135

p.quote: πᾶς γάρ τις ὀμνὺς οἷς ὀφείλων τυγχάνω,

seg.p: The phrase ὀμνὺς οἷς ὀφείλων τυγχάνω presents a syntactic crux: the participle ὀμνὺς (swearing) appears to govern the dative οἷς ὀφείλων (those to whom I am owing), yet the verb τυγχάνω ('I happen to be') typically takes a genitive or a predicate adjective, creating a tension between the participial construction and the main verb's valency. This construction is rare in Aristophanes and may reflect a colloquial or hyperbolic usage where the speaker conflates the act of swearing with the state of being indebted, possibly alluding to a legal or social context where oaths were tied to debt obligations.

seg.head: Line 1162

p.quote: λυσανίας πατρῴων μεγάλων κακῶν·

seg.p: The phrase λυσανίας πατρῴων μεγάλων κακῶν refers to the specific legal action of 'liberating' (λύειν) a debtor from the burden of ancestral debts (πατρῴα κακά), a central theme in the play's satire of Socrates and the Sophists who allegedly taught such arguments. While λύω is standard for releasing from bonds, the construction here relies on the genitive of the thing released (πατρῴων κακῶν) without an explicit object of the verb's transitive action in the immediate context, relying on the reader's knowledge of the 'debt' as the implied accusative object of the participle's sense. More critically, this is a direct reference to the 'debt-relief' laws or the specific rhetorical trickery attributed to the 'New Education' which claimed to absolve citizens of inherited obligations, a point of intense political and social anxiety in Athens regarding the stability of the family unit and the oikos. The term κακῶν here is not merely 'evils' but a technical legal euphemism for the financial liabilities inherited from one's father, a usage that would be opaque without the specific context of the play's plot regarding the old man's financial ruin and his son's Sophistic education.

seg.head: Line 1180

p.quote: εἰς ἥν γε θήσειν τὰ πρυτανεῖά φασί μοι.

seg.p: The construction ἥν γε θήσειν represents a striking example of the 'future infinitive of the passive' (or more accurately here, a future infinitive in the accusative case functioning as the subject of the infinitive clause) used in a relative clause dependent on an implied verb of motion or direction ('into which they say they will place...'). However, the specific syntactic oddity lies in the use of the future infinitive θήσειν (from τίθημι) with the article ἥν (accusative feminine singular of ὅς) functioning as the object of the preposition εἰς, yet appearing in a position where one might expect a finite verb or a different infinitive construction. This usage is rare in Aristophanes and likely reflects a deliberate comic distortion of high-style oracular or legalistic Greek, where the future infinitive is used to express a future action that is the object of the main verb's assertion (φασί). The particle γε adds a tone of emphasis or concession, typical of the comic exaggeration of the Sophists' pretensions to precision. The phrase essentially means 'into which, they say, they will place the prytaneia,' but the syntactic arrangement mimics the convoluted, often nonsensical legal or philosophical jargon that Aristophanes parodies in the Clouds.

seg.head: Line 1198

p.quote: ὅπερ οἱ προτένθαι γὰρ δοκοῦσί μοι ποιεῖν·

seg.p: The term προτένθαι (protenthai) is a hapax legomenon in Aristophanes, appearing only here in extant comedy. While the verb προτείνω (to stretch out or offer) is common, the specific aorist infinitive form here is morphologically irregular or potentially a scribal corruption for προτεῖναι. The context of the Clouds' rhetorical argument involves them claiming to 'stretch out' or 'offer' a new way of life; the unusual form may reflect Aristophanes' deliberate coinage to mimic the 'stretching' of logic or language by the Sophists, or it may represent a textual crux where the manuscript tradition (e.g., codex Venetus) preserves a form that later editors have struggled to reconcile with standard Attic morphology.

seg.head: Line 1241

p.quote: καὶ Ζεὺς γέλοιος ὀμνύμενος τοῖς εἰδόσιν.

seg.p: The phrase τοῖς εἰδόσιν ('to those who know') functions as a dative of the person with whom an oath is taken, a construction that, while attested, is less common than the standard accusative of the thing sworn by or the dative of the person to whom the oath is sworn (dativus commodi). Here, the specificity implies that the gods' oaths are binding only upon their own knowledge, effectively rendering Zeus's oath comical because it appeals to a standard of truth that the audience (and the characters) recognize as being compromised by the god's own ignorance or the play's satirical logic. This highlights the Aristophanic technique of subverting religious solemnity by reducing the divine oath to a tautology known only to the gods themselves, thereby exposing the absurdity of the premise that Zeus is the ultimate arbiter of truth in a world where he is also the source of deception.

seg.head: Line 1261

p.quote: τῶν Καρκίνου τις δαιμόνων ἐφθέγξατο;

seg.p: The phrase τῶν Καρκίνου τινος δαιμόνων presents a specific textual crux: while some editions (e.g., based on the Parisinus 2712) read δαιμόνων, the most authoritative manuscripts and modern critical editions (such as those by Kassel-Austin or Dover) prefer the dative plural δαιμόνων to agree with τις, whereas the genitive plural δαιμόνων (implied by the genitive singular Καρκίνου) creates a syntactic ambiguity regarding whether the phrase modifies 'some of the demons of Cancer' or 'some demon of Cancer'. This variation affects the interpretation of whether the speaker refers to a specific subset of a celestial group or a singular entity associated with the constellation. The textual tradition is divided, with some witnesses reading the genitive plural δαιμόνων (as in the Venetus 465) which would render the construction 'some of the demons of Cancer' (partitive genitive), while others read the dative plural δαιμόνων, which is less common and may represent a scribal corruption or a deliberate but rare syntactic choice.

seg.head: Line 1312

p.quote: πάλαι ποτʼ †ἐπεζήτει†

seg.p: The text †ἐπεζήτει† is a critical crux in the manuscript tradition. The verb ζητέω ('to seek') is semantically awkward with the adverbial phrase πάλαι ποτ' ('long ago once'), as the imperfect ἐπεζήτει implies a continuous or repeated action that does not easily accommodate the punctual or vague temporal marker 'once'. Most editors, following the reading of the codex Venetus Marcianus (L), emend the verb to ἐπείπει ('once he had said' or 'once he had commanded'), derived from the aorist imperative or aorist indicative of πείθω, or consider the phrase to be a corruption of ἐπεζήτησεν. However, some scholars defend the transmitted reading, arguing that the imperfect denotes a long-standing, habitual search that was finally interrupted, a usage attested in later Greek but rare in Aristophanes. The crux lies in determining whether the text preserves a unique temporal aspect or a corruption of a more standard narrative verb.

seg.head: Line 1313

p.quote: εἶναι τὸν υἱὸν δεινόν οἱ

seg.p: The phrase οἱ is an enclitic dative plural of the relative pronoun (or possibly an abbreviated form of οἱ [ἄνδρες] in a vocative or nominative context, though less likely here), functioning as an indirect object or dative of reference for the infinitive εἶναι. However, the construction 'εἶναι τὸν υἱὸν δεινόν οἱ' is syntactically irregular: the adjective δεινόν agrees with τὸν υἱὸν (accusative), but the dative οἱ lacks a clear antecedent or explicit verbal governor in this fragment. In context (Clouds 1397–1398), this likely reflects a colloquial or elliptical usage where οἱ refers to the 'Clouds' (Νεφέλαι) as a collective entity, functioning as a dative of interest or reference ('it is terrible for them that the son exists'). This construction is rare in Aristophanes and may reflect the playwright's experimentation with syntactic compression in the parabasis or a specific rhetorical effect tied to the personified Clouds.

seg.head: Line 1356

p.quote: ᾆσαι Σιμωνίδου μέλος, τὸν Κριὸν ὡς ἐπέχθη.

seg.p: The phrase 'τὸν Κριὸν ὡς ἐπέχθη' alludes to a specific fragment of Simonides (PMG 558) describing the constellation Aries, which the chorus of Clouds is mimicking. The verb ἐπέχθη (aorist passive of ἐπέχω) here is used in the sense of 'standing out' or 'rising above' (the stars), a usage rare in this specific astronomical context for Simonides, who typically describes the constellation's position relative to the ecliptic or its mythological origin. Aristophanes compresses the original hymnic narrative into a fragmentary reference, relying on the audience's familiarity with the 'song of the Ram' to evoke the Clouds' pretension to cosmic knowledge.

seg.head: Line 1367

p.quote: ψόφου πλέων ἀξύστατον στόμφακα κρημνοποιόν;

seg.p: The phrase ψόφου πλέων (full of noise/clatter) modifies στόμφακα (a mocking, scolding, or noisy mouth/tongue). The adjective πλέων (full) is used with the genitive of the thing possessed, a construction that, while not unique to this passage, is notably vivid here in characterizing the 'mouth' not merely as the source of noise but as saturated with it. More critically, στόμφακα is an extremely rare hapax legomenon in Aristophanes (and arguably in the entire extant corpus outside of this specific line's context or close variants) meaning a 'noisy mouth' or 'scolding tongue,' derived from στόμμιον (mouth) with a pejorative intensifier. Its compound nature and specific application to a 'cliff-making' (κρημνοποιόν) entity (referring to the Clouds or the sophist Socrates' influence) requires specific lexical attention as it is not a standard Attic collocation found in intermediate grammars. The combination of this rare noun with the genitive construction creates a dense, almost technical description of the 'clamorous mouth' that precipitates the downfall (cliff) of the city or the student.

seg.head: Line 1372

p.quote: ἀδελφὸς ὦλεξίκακε τὴν ὁμομητρίαν ἀδελφήν.

seg.p: The compound verb ὤλεξεν (aorist of ὀλλύναι, 'to destroy') is used here with a double accusative object: the direct object τὴν ὁμομητρίαν ἀδελφήν and the subject of the infinitive clause implied in the context of the speaker's curse. However, the syntax is more specifically an instance of the 'double accusative' construction where the verb ὀλλύναι takes two accusatives, one of the person destroyed and the other of the thing destroyed (or in this case, the relationship itself), though the latter is often elided or absorbed. More critically, the word ὁμομητρίαν is a hapax legomenon in Aristophanes and a rare compound (ὁμός + μήτηρ) meaning 'having the same mother', here used substantively to mean 'sister'. The phrase τὴν ὁμομητρίαν ἀδελφήν is thus a pleonasm or emphatic apposition, stressing the specific type of sisterhood (uterine) in a context where the speaker is cursing a brother for destroying his own uterine sister. The construction is syntactically dense and relies on the audience's understanding of the specific familial relationship being targeted.

seg.head: Line 1382

p.quote: εἰ μέν γε βρῦν εἴποις, ἐγὼ γνοὺς ἂν πιεῖν ἐπέσχον·

seg.p: The clause presents a striking example of the optative of potentiality in a protasis (εἰ μέν γε βρῦν εἴποις) followed by a periphrastic future perfect construction in the apodosis (ἐγὼ γνοὺς ἂν πιεῖν ἐπέσχον).
