The verb ἐπέσχον (aorist indicative) here functions as a gnomic aorist or a specific historical aorist of the narrator's past action, yet it is governed by the conditional particle ἄν attached to the participle γνοὺς, creating a hybrid construction where the apodosis describes a completed action (holding back) that was contingent upon a hypothetical condition. This syntactic blending of the aorist indicative with the optative conditional framework is rare in Attic prose and distinctively characteristic of Aristophanic comedy, where the speaker (Strepsiades) mimics the convoluted, hyper-logical rhetoric of the Sophists while simultaneously admitting to a literal, physical reaction to the absurdity of the word 'cloud' (βρῦν) being spoken.

seg.head: Line 1387

p.quote: χεζητιῴην, οὐκ ἔτλης

seg.p: The form χεζητιῴην is a rare Doric aorist optative of ζητέω (or possibly a dialectal variant of ζητήσοιμι), reflecting the strong Doric coloring of Aristophanes' comic dialogue here; the juxtaposition of this optative with the aorist indicative ἔτλης creates a syntactic tension that may signal a shift from wishful thinking to immediate reproach, a feature characteristic of Aristophanic dialogue where grammatical mood often tracks the speaker's rhetorical pivot.

seg.head: Line 1397

p.quote: σὸν ἔργον ὦ καινῶν ἐπῶν κινητὰ καὶ μοχλευτὰ

seg.p: The phrase κινητὰ καὶ μοχλευτὰ presents a striking syntactic and semantic anomaly. While the first participle (kinēta) functions adjectivally to describe 'works' (ergon) as 'shakable' or 'unstable'—a standard metaphor for rhetorical instability—the second (mochleuta) is a hapax legomenon in this context, derived from mochleuo ('to work a lever' or 'to pry'). Aristophanes here employs a rare, compound verbal noun in the accusative to personify the 'works' as active agents of prying or manipulation, creating a deliberate pun on the physical act of leverage and the rhetorical 'leveraging' of arguments. This construction is not merely a standard adjectival modifier but a marked rhetorical device where the abstract 'work' is grammatically treated as a mechanical operator, reflecting the play's broader satire on the Sophists' manipulation of language.

seg.head: Line 1407

p.quote: ἵππων τρέφειν τέθριππον ἢ τυπτόμενον ἐπιτριβῆναι.

seg.p: The phrase τυπτόμενον ἐπιτριβῆναι presents a striking syntactic and semantic difficulty: τυπτόμενον (a present middle/passive participle of τυπτω) typically means 'being struck' or 'beaten', yet here it modifies the action of ἐπιτριβῆναι ('to be rubbed upon'). This construction implies a paradoxical image of a horse being 'rubbed while being struck,' which has led scholars to conjecture that τυπτόμενον may be a corruption of τριβόμενον ('being rubbed') or that the text preserves a deliberate, ironic wordplay on the physical abuse of the horse in the training regimen. The ambiguity is significant because it touches on the literal versus metaphorical understanding of the horse's suffering in the context of the Sophists' absurd teachings.

seg.head: Line 1466

p.quote: ἀπολεῖς μετʼ ἐμοῦ ʼλθών, οἳ σὲ κἄμʼ ἐξηπάτων.

seg.p: The pronoun οἳ functions as a relative pronoun with an antecedent that is not explicitly stated in the immediate clause but is supplied from the context of the preceding dialogue (likely referring to the 'Clouds' or the 'New Learning' personified). This usage of οἳ to refer to an abstract or personified collective entity, rather than a concrete plural noun, is a characteristic feature of Aristophanic personification that requires the reader to infer the antecedent from the dramatic context rather than the syntax of the isolated sentence.

seg.head: Line 1471

p.quote: Δῖνος βασιλεύει τὸν Δίʼ ἐξεληλακώς.

seg.p: The participle ἐξεληλακώς (perfect active) modifies Δῖνος (Dinos, the personification of the Whirlwind), creating a striking paradox: Dinos, who has forcibly expelled Zeus, now claims the throne. This construction relies on the reader recognizing Dinos not merely as a meteorological force but as the protagonist of the play's 'New Learning' who has successfully usurped the divine order, replacing Zeus with the 'Clouds' (Νεφέλαι) and their new theology. The perfect tense emphasizes the completed, irreversible nature of this coup, a central thematic pivot in the parabasis and the subsequent trial of Socrates.

seg.head: Line 1490

p.quote: ἐμοὶ δὲ δᾷδʼ ἐνεγκάτω τις ἡμμένην,

seg.p: The participle ἡμμένην (perfect passive participle of ἱμνύμι, 'to kindle') is rare in this specific morphological form; the more common perfect active form ἡμμένη is not attested here, and the perfect passive 'having been kindled' is semantically necessary to describe the torch as already lit and ready to be carried, contrasting with the future action of the carrier. This construction highlights the state of the object rather than the action of lighting, which is crucial for the stage direction implied in the line.

seg.head: Line 1496

p.quote: διαλεπτολογοῦμαι ταῖς δοκοῖς τῆς οἰκίας;

seg.p: The hapax legomenon διαλεπτολογοῦμαι (dia-lepto-logoumai) is a compound verb unique to this passage, formed from διά, λεπτός, and λέγω. While λεπτός typically denotes 'fine' or 'thin' in physical descriptions (e.g., fine air, thin air), here it modifies the manner of speaking to imply 'subtle' or 'sophisticated' argumentation. The prefix διά- suggests a thorough or scattered discourse. This neologism is a deliberate Aristophanic coinage mocking the Socratic habit of dissecting language and reality into increasingly abstract, 'thin' components, contrasting sharply with the concrete 'rafters' (δοκαί) of the house mentioned in the dative of separation.
